solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Praise Obama’s final assertion in speech (7)

indicators.note: Obama's final letter is his last one, A
spoken out, 'a claim' is heard as one word

blocks.note: the two words spoken together run into a single word of the same sound

annotation.surface: A tribute to a president's last pronouncement in an address.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Obama's final assertion' reads as his last statement in office; it is really his last letter followed by a claim, run together as one sound.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, as a verb: to hail or applaud someone publicly.

entries.clue: Open article on revolutionary period of British rule (4)

indicators.note: something that revolves turns round, so the word is read backwards

blocks.note: the RAJ, British rule in India, turned round

annotation.surface: A newspaper piece on a rebellious chapter of the colonial era.
annotation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' puts the article above the rest. 'Revolutionary' suggests uprisings against the Raj; it only turns the word round.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for a door or window left partly open.

entries.clue: Two blokes meeting pedlar of old (7)

blocks.note: the second bloke is a man

annotation.surface: A pair of men bumping into an old-fashioned travelling salesman.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Two blokes' supplies two synonyms for bloke, one after the other.
annotation.definitionFit: A chapman was a hawker or itinerant dealer, a word now found mostly in older English.

entries.clue: Clearly the Speaker’s given permission (5)

indicators.note: the word as a speaker pronounces it, not as it is written

blocks.note: allowed = given permission; say it and hear a different spelling

annotation.surface: The Commons Speaker has plainly granted leave.
annotation.walkthrough: 'The Speaker' looks like the Speaker of the House of Commons, who does grant permission to speak; here it just marks a word that is heard, not read.
annotation.definitionFit: Speaking aloud means speaking audibly, so that one is heard clearly.

entries.clue: Hide from agent’s ruler briefly (8)

indicators.note: cut short, so the last letter goes

blocks.note: a mole is a spy planted inside an organisation, with the 's

annotation.surface: A spy concealing himself from the monarch he is betraying.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Hide' looks like a verb for the fugitive agent; it is the noun, an animal's skin.
annotation.definitionFit: Moleskin is the skin of a mole, a hide; the word also names a heavy cotton fabric.

entries.clue: Recreation area in grounds at last, with space for people playing (7)

indicators.note: take the final letter of grounds

blocks.note: the orchestra pit, where musicians play

annotation.surface: A description of a playground with room set aside for games.
annotation.walkthrough: 'People playing' suggests children at games; the players are musicians, and their space is the orchestra pit below a stage.
annotation.definitionFit: A sandpit is a patch of sand for children to play in, a small recreation area.

entries.clue: Misdemeanour outside pub by one not easily understood (6)

indicators.note: SIN goes round the outside of PH
'by' is the multiplication sign, as in 3 by 4, written X

blocks.note: PH, public house, as on maps

annotation.surface: A minor offence committed outside a pub by somebody who mumbles.
annotation.walkthrough: 'By one' reads as 'committed by someone'; 'by' is the times sign X and 'one' starts the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A sphinx is an enigmatic, inscrutable person, after the riddling monster of Greek myth.

entries.clue: Remains in northern French city, capital of country (9)

indicators.note: ASH goes inside N and VILLE

blocks.note: ash is what remains after burning
ville is French for town or city

annotation.surface: Relics found in a city in the north of France, which turns out to be a national capital.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Capital of country' looks like a nation's capital; the country is country music, whose capital is Nashville, Tennessee.
annotation.definitionFit: Nashville is home to the Grand Ole Opry and the country-music industry, so it is called the capital of country music.

entries.clue: Turning up about noon, sneak something to drink (7)

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning up means reading from bottom to top

blocks.note: to slip in or out is to sneak

annotation.surface: Someone arriving around midday and slipping off for a quiet drink.
annotation.walkthrough: The three pieces are assembled as RENSLIP and then turned upwards.
annotation.definitionFit: Pilsner is a pale lager, originally from Pilsen in Bohemia.

entries.clue: Sixty other Crees resettled (10)

indicators.note: the letters are moved to a new arrangement

annotation.surface: Sixty more members of the Cree nation moved to new land.
annotation.walkthrough: The Cree are a First Nations people of Canada, which makes 'resettled' sound like a historical relocation.
annotation.definitionFit: A score is twenty, so three score is sixty, as in 'threescore years and ten'.

entries.clue: A toff introducing island’s religious leader (9)

indicators.note: the toff takes the island into himself

blocks.note: a yah is a posh British person, from their 'yah' for 'yes'
an atoll is a ring-shaped coral island

annotation.surface: An upper-class gentleman presenting an islander to a cleric.
annotation.walkthrough: YAH is a British nickname for a posh person, mimicking their accent; the 's after island stands for 'is' and joins wordplay to definition.
annotation.definitionFit: An ayatollah is a senior Shia Muslim cleric in Iran.

entries.clue: Notes resistance from the Sun (5)

blocks.note: so and la, two notes of the sol-fa scale
R, the physics symbol for resistance

annotation.surface: A scientist logs the resistance of radiation coming from the Sun.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Notes' looks like jotted observations; it is two notes of the do-re-mi scale.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain adjective: solar energy is energy from the Sun, from Latin sol.

entries.clue: Way in which one might get promotion? (7,6)

definitions.text: Way in which one might get promotion?

blocks.note: the surface wants a method; the setter means a road, a street name

blocks.clueFragment: in which one might get promotion?
blocks.note: the surface wants a step up at work; the setter means promotion of products, advertising

annotation.surface: A career question: what is the route to getting promoted?
annotation.walkthrough: 'Way' reads as a method and 'promotion' as a step up at work; the way is a street and the promotion is advertising.
annotation.definitionFit: Madison Avenue in Manhattan is so tied to advertising that its name stands for the whole industry.

entries.clue: Dogged engineer enters pits (10)

indicators.note: to engineer is to rearrange or contrive, here the letters

annotation.surface: A determined engineer goes down into the mines.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Engineer' looks like the person entering the pits; it is a verb telling you to rework the next two words.
annotation.definitionFit: Dogged and persistent both mean refusing to give up.

entries.clue: Articles in Die Zeit carrying little weight for scientist (8)

indicators.note: the two articles hold the weight between them

blocks.note: ein is the German indefinite article, twice
ST, the abbreviation for stone, a British weight of 14 lb

annotation.surface: Some pieces in a German newspaper that barely matter to a scientist.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Die Zeit' is a German weekly, which tells you the articles are German words, not newspaper stories. 'Little weight' is a weight written short, not an unimportant one.
annotation.definitionFit: Albert Einstein, the physicist of relativity, fittingly German-born.

entries.clue: Kitchen assistant’s absurd pretension alienating staff at first (3,6)

indicators.note: absurd letters are nonsense until rearranged
alienating means pushing away, so the letter is removed
only the first letter of staff is taken

blocks.note: lose S, the first letter of staff

annotation.surface: A kitchen worker's pompous airs put the rest of the staff off.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Kitchen assistant' looks like a junior cook; it is a gadget. The 's stands for 'is', joining definition to wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A tin opener is a kitchen tool for opening cans, which assists the cook.

entries.clue: Cardinal possibly involved in debacle? Richelieu (6)

indicators.note: the answer is wrapped up inside the next words

annotation.surface: Asking whether a cardinal had a hand in a fiasco, and naming Richelieu.
annotation.walkthrough: Richelieu was a real cardinal, so he looks like the answer to the question; he only lends the last three letters.
annotation.definitionFit: A cardinal is a senior cleric of the Catholic Church, hence 'possibly'.

entries.clue: Poirot’s a hero! (8)

blocks.note: Agatha Christie's detective is Hercule Poirot

annotation.surface: A fan exclaiming that the Belgian detective is a real hero.
annotation.walkthrough: The detective's first name plus the possessive makes the Greek hero; 'Poirot's' reads as 'Poirot is'.
annotation.definitionFit: Hercules is the hero of Greek and Roman myth famous for his twelve labours.

entries.clue: Undernourished people in South American city (6)

indicators.note: people living in a city are inside it, so KIN is placed inside the letters for the city

blocks.note: one's kin are one's people, family

annotation.surface: Hungry folk living in a city in South America.
annotation.walkthrough: 'South American city' reads as one place like Lima; it splits into S and an American city, NY.
annotation.definitionFit: Skinny means very thin, as someone undernourished is.

entries.clue: One crossword setter nicking a drink — can you believe that! (7)

indicators.note: to nick is to steal, so ME takes A GIN into itself

blocks.note: the setter refers to themselves as me

annotation.surface: A puzzle compiler caught pinching a drink, to the reader's astonishment.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Crossword setter' giving ME is a standard trick: the setter is the one talking to you.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Imagine!' is an exclamation of amazement, just like 'can you believe that!'

entries.clue: Father for one’s enthralled by Trump (8)

indicators.note: held captive inside the next word

blocks.note: to trump is to better, to outdo
e.g. = for example, for one; the 's is 'is'

annotation.surface: A priest dazzled by a certain American president.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Trump' invites the president; it is the verb, to better. EG goes after the B.
annotation.definitionFit: To beget is to father a child, so the one who does it is the father; the word also means any originator.

entries.clue: Hot saké ordered? You can bet on it (3,4)

indicators.note: the saké is ordered in a bar, but ordered also means arranged, so the letters are sorted into a new sequence

annotation.surface: A diner orders warm rice wine, and a friend wagers they'll like it.
annotation.walkthrough: The Oaks is a British flat horse race for fillies, run at Epsom each summer.
annotation.definitionFit: The Oaks is a classic horse race, so it is something you can place a bet on.

entries.clue: Backing withdrawal of police for now (3,3)

indicators.note: a withdrawal is a pulling back, so the word goes back to front

blocks.note: the Met, London's Metropolitan Police, turned back

annotation.surface: Supporting the police pulling out, at least for the time being.
annotation.walkthrough: The Met is London's Metropolitan Police. 'Backing' looks like the reversal indicator but it means PRO; 'withdrawal' does the turning.
annotation.definitionFit: Pro tem, short for Latin pro tempore, means for the time being.

entries.clue: Dubious goings-on in second instrumental run-through (5,8)

annotation.surface: Something shady happening at an orchestra's second rehearsal.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Second instrumental run-through' reads as a second rehearsal; it splits into S, an instrument, and a practice.
annotation.definitionFit: Sharp practice is dishonest or barely legal dealing.

entries.clue: Fire associate that’s lost millions (5)

indicators.note: a word that has lost something no longer has it, so the M comes out

blocks.note: to mingle is to associate with others

annotation.surface: A firm sacking a colleague who cost it millions.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fire associate' reads as dismissing a partner; 'Fire' is the definition, a hearth fire.
annotation.definitionFit: An ingle is a fire on a domestic hearth, as in inglenook.

entries.clue: Feature of good health? Not half! (4)

indicators.note: only half the phrase is kept

blocks.note: an old-fashioned British drinking toast, a doubled word meaning 'good health!'

annotation.surface: A question about what marks out good health, answered with an emphatic 'Not half!'
annotation.walkthrough: 'Not half!' is British slang for 'very much so'; here it means literally half. Chin-chin is an old-fashioned toast.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: features in the sense of parts of the face, of which this is one.

entries.clue: Unsophisticated, backward-looking spa town (5)

indicators.note: looking backwards means reading the word from its end

annotation.surface: A description of a provincial resort stuck in the past.
annotation.walkthrough: Évian-les-Bains is a French spa town on Lake Geneva, known for its bottled water.
annotation.definitionFit: Evian is a spa town famous for its mineral springs.

entries.clue: Daily could be great help (9)

indicators.note: the letters could become the answer if rearranged

annotation.surface: A daily cleaner might be a big help around the house.
annotation.walkthrough: A 'daily' in British usage is a cleaner who comes in each day, which is the picture; here it is a daily newspaper, the Daily Telegraph.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a daily is a newspaper published every day, and this London one is among the best known.

entries.clue: Proposition English troops to infiltrate enemy (7)

indicators.note: to get inside, so E and OR go inside THEM

blocks.note: OR, other ranks, soldiers who are not officers

annotation.surface: A plan to send English soldiers behind enemy lines.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Proposition' looks like a battle plan; it is a statement proved in mathematics.
annotation.definitionFit: The mathematical sense of proposition: a statement put forward to be proved, as in Euclid.

entries.clue: Tramples over partner’s earlier issue (7)

blocks.note: a two-word phrase for walking over something, with the space closed up
a spouse's son from a previous relationship

annotation.surface: Someone walking all over a spouse's child from an earlier marriage.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Issue' means offspring, not a problem. The first sense is two words, STEPS ON, run together.
annotation.definitionFit: A stepson is one's partner's son from an earlier relationship, their earlier issue.
